claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by rapid and simultaneous reduction or nucleation of all metal precursors.
Nearly simultaneous reduction or nucleation kinetically traps the metals in a single solid-solution phase.
Atomic diffusion can induce phase separation in noble metal–containing high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed starting material is a uniformly mixed precursor in which the metal ions are homogeneously distributed.
A rapid, high-intensity thermal or chemical reduction protocol will induce nearly simultaneous nucleation of all metal species.
Simultaneous atomic-level nucleation dynamically locks the elements into a homogeneous solid solution.
Rapid reduction minimizes the time available for atomic diffusion.
Suppressing atomic diffusion suppresses elemental or phase segregation.
Slower synthesis kinetics provide enough time for thermodynamically driven segregation.
Rapid reduction will produce nanoparticles with a uniform, single-phase structure and evenly distributed elements.
Slower reduction will lead to phase separation and elemental segregation.
Slower reduction may produce uncontrolled nanoparticle morphologies.
Moderate reduction or conventional heating permits sufficient time for diffusive segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to noble-metal systems whose components have similar reduction potentials and nucleation kinetics.
The mechanism may fail when elemental properties are very dissimilar or thermodynamic driving forces for segregation are overwhelmingly strong.
The threshold reduction rate required for homogeneous nucleation has not been quantitatively established.
